exp20v2-ethics.audit:
Ethics, Persuasion & Trust

Auditing Your Own Product

What would an honest audit of my product's persuasion find?

1. Nine days before the term sheet closes

On the morning of March 22, 2026, Kabir Malhotra, head of product at Parakh Wellness, a Bangalore-based sleep and meditation app with 68,000 monthly active users, opened a growth deck he had not asked for. Parakh's board would meet on March 31 to decide whether to close a Series B round; the lead investor's term sheet was contingent on 30-day retention crossing 34%, up from the 30% the app had held for two quarters. The growth team's proposal to close that gap in nine days had three parts: shrink the "Skip today" button on the daily reminder to a pale grey link, add a line of copy under it that read "Your 41-day streak will reset — are you sure?", and turn on a feature already built and dormant since December: a push notification reading "Your friend Rohan meditated today," drawn from the phone contacts Parakh's onboarding flow had asked permission to read for a since-abandoned "find friends" feature.

Kabir's discomfort was not abstract. Three weeks earlier, a business daily had run an investigation into a lending app whose forced-continuity checkout the Central Consumer Protection Authority was examining under its November 2023 guidelines on dark patterns — the first time Kabir had seen an Indian regulator name specific manipulative UI tactics rather than gesture vaguely at "unfair practices." He did not know whether any of Parakh's three loops crossed that line. He knew he was about to find out under time pressure, from the same team whose bonus depended on the answer being no. What he needed was not an opinion. It was a method he could defend to the board, to a journalist, and to himself.

2. The idea: what an audit actually checks

An audit of your own product's persuasion is a structured walk through every loop that makes users come back, mechanism by mechanism, checked first against a catalogue of manipulative UI tactics and then against a set of ethical tests — so that what you find is evidence, not a feeling. It exists because three separate bodies of work, each useful alone, are dangerous half-used. Nir Eyal's 2014 book Hooked gave product teams the Hook Model: a loop of external or internal trigger, action, variable reward, and investment that explains why habit-forming products keep people returning. Used alone, it is a design tool with no conscience — it tells you how to build a hook, not whether you should. Harry Brignull's 2010 dark-patterns taxonomy named specific tactics — nagging, confirmshaming, sneaking, forced action, false urgency — that make hooks manipulative rather than merely persuasive. Used alone, it is a checklist that tells you a tactic is present but not how much it matters. The Markkula Center for Applied Ethics at Santa Clara University's five ethical lenses — rights, justice, utilitarian, common good, virtue — give you a way to weigh what the taxonomy finds against real human stakes, rather than treating every flagged tactic as equally serious.

The audit is the discipline of running all three together: the Hook canvas as the map of your own mechanisms, the taxonomy as the metal detector, the lenses as the judge. The sentence Kabir could repeat in the board meeting without sounding glib was this one.

An honest audit doesn't ask whether the product works. It asks whether you'd be comfortable explaining exactly how it works to the person it works on.

3. How it actually works

The audit begins with the artefact most product teams already have and rarely re-read: the Hook canvas for each major loop. Kabir pulled three canvases from Parakh's growth wiki — the daily streak reminder, the dormant friend-activity push, and the subscription cancellation flow — and, for each, wrote down not the intended effect but the literal mechanism: the exact copy, the exact data used, the exact default. This step is the one teams skip, because it is tedious and because the canvas usually only records what the loop is meant to accomplish, not how it accomplishes it.

Next, each mechanism is checked line by line against the dark-patterns taxonomy's named categories — nagging (repeated interruption), confirmshaming (guilt-worded refusal), sneaking (using data or charging money without clear disclosure), obstruction (making an exit harder than an entry), and forced action (bundling a wanted action with an unwanted one). A mechanism can match more than one category, and the point of this pass is coverage, not judgment — everything gets flagged for now.

Only the flagged mechanisms move to the third step: each is run through the Markkula lenses. The rights lens asks whether the user could reasonably be said to have consented to what is actually happening. The justice lens asks who bears the cost and whether it falls disproportionately on people least able to absorb it. The common-good lens asks what happens if every app in the category does this. The utilitarian lens weighs total benefit against total harm. The virtue lens asks what kind of company this makes you, regardless of outcome. A mechanism that survives all five is kept; one that fails even one gets scored, not automatically killed — because severity and reach still have to be weighed, which is the step most teams do implicitly and badly, by gut feel, under deadline. The audit makes that step explicit and numeric.

What practitioners usually skip

Two steps rarely appear in a rushed audit and both cost Kabir later if he skipped them: recording the current, unaltered metrics for each loop before touching anything, so that any later change in retention can be attributed rather than assumed; and having someone who did not build the loop run the taxonomy pass, because the person who wrote "are you sure?" under a shrunk button no longer sees it as friction.

4. The worked example: two ways to rank the same three loops

Kabir scored Parakh's three flagged loops using a simple risk index: reach (the share of Parakh's 68,000 MAU the loop touches) multiplied by a severity weight (1 for a single mild tactic, up to 3 for obstruction or sneaking) multiplied by a deception factor from the rights-lens check (1.0 for full disclosure, rising toward 3.0 as consent becomes less real).

Table 1 — Risk index weighted by reach (Pass 1)
LoopReachSeverityDeceptionRisk index
Daily streak reminder (confirmshaming copy)41,200 / 68,000 = 60.6%21.40.606 × 2 × 1.4 = 1.70
"Rohan meditated today" push (contacts used without fresh consent)12,500 / 68,000 = 18.4%32.10.184 × 3 × 2.1 = 1.16
Cancellation flow (three forced retention screens)900 / 68,000 = 1.3%32.80.013 × 3 × 2.8 = 0.11

Read this way, the streak reminder is the biggest problem, purely because it touches six users for every one the friend-push reaches. That was the growth team's own instinct — fix the thing everyone sees. But Kabir ran a second pass, dropping reach from the formula entirely and scoring only severity times deception, on the argument that a regulator or a journalist does not discover a dark pattern proportionally to how many users hit it; a single well-documented case of using unconsented contact data is a front-page story regardless of scale.

Table 2 — Risk index weighted by severity × deception only (Pass 2)
LoopSeverity × Deception
Daily streak reminder2 × 1.4 = 2.8
"Rohan meditated today" push3 × 2.1 = 6.3
Cancellation flow3 × 2.8 = 8.4

The ranking inverts. Under Pass 2 the cancellation flow — the loop touching barely 1.3% of users — is the most serious, because it combines a high severity tactic with the weakest consent. Neither pass is "the" right answer; each answers a different question. Pass 1 estimates operational exposure — how many relationships this is quietly damaging. Pass 2 estimates reputational and regulatory exposure — how bad the worst single documented instance would look. A defensible audit reports both and says which risk the business is actually more exposed to right now, rather than picking whichever ranking is more convenient.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

The auditor cannot be the loop's owner

The person who wrote the confirmshaming copy genuinely does not see it as guilt — they see it as "reminding users what they'll lose." This is not dishonesty; it is proximity. An audit run entirely inside the team that built the hooks will systematically under-flag its own work, which is why the taxonomy pass needs at least one reader who did not build any of the three loops.

Legal and ethical are different lines

Parakh's contacts-based push may or may not violate India's data-protection rules depending on exactly what consent language the original onboarding flow used. That is a legal question with a lawyer's answer. Whether it is right to nudge a stranger's meditation habit using their friend's private contact list, even if legal, is a separate question the rights lens answers on its own terms. Passing a compliance review is not the same finding as passing an ethics audit.

The same tactic can be manipulation or information

"Only 3 seats left" is a dark pattern — false urgency — when the number is invented, and honest, useful information when it is real inventory. The taxonomy names the shape of a tactic; it cannot tell you, by pattern-matching alone, whether a given instance is true. That check is a separate, boring step: go look at the underlying data.

Intent is not a defense

"We didn't design it to manipulate anyone" answers a question the audit did not ask. The Markkula lenses evaluate the effect on the person on the other end of the mechanism, not the state of mind of the person who shipped it. A well-meaning team can build a manipulative loop by accident, and the audit exists precisely to catch what good intentions miss.

Reach-weighting and severity-weighting answer different questions

As Table 1 and Table 2 showed, changing one input in the same formula can flip the ranking entirely. A team that runs the audit once, with one weighting, and treats the resulting list as objective has quietly made a policy choice — which risk matters more — without naming it as one.

The audit finds problems; it does not design the fix

Knowing that the friend-push fails the rights lens tells Kabir to stop it or add explicit re-consent. It does not tell him what replaces the retention value that loop was providing. That is a separate design problem, and treating the audit's output as a finished answer skips it.

A single audit expires

Every AB test the growth team ships after this audit is a new mechanism the audit never saw. Hooks drift one small experiment at a time — the frog-boiling problem — so a one-time cleanup before a board meeting is not the same as an ongoing practice.

6. Where this looks different

In a consumer app like Parakh, the hooks act directly on the sole decision-maker's emotions — streaks, social proof, guilt — so the audit is mostly about individual psychological pressure. In a B2B product like Nirikshan Cloud, a Pune-based workflow-automation platform, the person who feels the hook — an operations admin nudged toward adding more paid seats — is often not the person who signed the contract or pays the invoice, so the audit has to ask whose consent was actually obtained, not just whether a click happened. In a two-sided marketplace like Tehkikat Bazaar, a Lucknow grocery platform, the audit has to run twice: once for the tactics aimed at buyers (a "3 left in stock" label that never checks real inventory) and once for tactics aimed at sellers (a commission change buried in a settings update sellers never open), because a loop that looks clean from one side of the marketplace can be manipulative from the other.

Stage matters as much as product type. An early-stage team, six months old, usually inherits hooks wholesale from a growth playbook or a competitor's screenshots, with no one having asked whether each mechanism was appropriate for this specific product — the risk there is ignorance. A large company running hundreds of simultaneous experiments faces a different risk: no single change looks manipulative, but the cumulative product, OKR quarter by OKR quarter, has drifted somewhere no one decided to go. The audit has to be built into the release process itself at that stage, not run as a rescue mission before a board meeting.

7. Common mistakes

Table 3 — What the mistake looks like from outside, and the cheapest way to catch it
MistakeSymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Claiming a clean bill without running the taxonomy"We don't really have dark patterns here"Conflating intent with effectHand the flow cold to five outside users and watch where they hesitate or misclick
Producing a long flag list nobody acts onAudit doc read once, never revisitedNo severity × reach scoring, so nothing outranks anything elseForce a single ranked top three before the meeting ends
Letting the loop's builder run the audit aloneEvery flagged item gets explained awayProximity bias mistaken for expertiseHave someone from support or legal shadow-run it independently and compare lists
Softening copy instead of the mechanismGuilt language removed, contacts still read without fresh consentTreating dark patterns as a tone problem, not a design problemAsk: would this still be fine written in plain language in the terms of service?

8. What good looks like

At Parakh, good looked like Kabir asking a product manager from an unrelated squad, who had touched none of the three loops, to run the taxonomy pass independently and compare notes before the board meeting — the two lists agreed on all three flags. Good looked like presenting both risk rankings from Table 1 and Table 2 rather than the one that was more flattering, and being explicit that the business was choosing to treat regulatory exposure, not raw reach, as the priority this quarter. Good looked like killing the friend-activity push entirely rather than softening its copy, since no wording fix repairs a rights-lens failure caused by the underlying data use. And it looked like proposing, in the same meeting, that any new loop above a minimum reach threshold pass this same three-step check before launch — turning a one-time audit into the standing gate the topic exists to unlock.

9. What Kabir decided

Kabir walked into the March 31 board meeting having kept the streak reminder with softened copy, killed the friend-activity push outright, and left the cancellation flow's structure in place while removing its most obstructive screen — a decision the severity-weighted ranking made hard to avoid defending honestly. He proposed the audit become a quarterly gate rather than a pre-board scramble. Retention did not reach 34% that quarter on the strength of the surviving loops alone, but the round closed anyway, on the strength of an answer the board had not expected a product head to have ready: not "our metrics are fine" but "here is exactly where we drew the line, and why."

What Kabir needed to learn next was the dark-patterns taxonomy in enough depth to name a mechanism precisely rather than approximately — vague labels like "manipulative" convince no one in a board meeting who wants specifics — and the Markkula lenses in enough depth to run all five quickly rather than stopping at whichever one felt most comfortable that day.

Sit with these two questions.

Which loop in your own product would fail if you had to explain its exact mechanism, in plain language, to the person it works on — not its outcome, its mechanism?

Who other than the person who built a hook should be the one deciding, on a recurring schedule, whether it still deserves to exist?

Ethics, Trust & Compliance › Ethics, Persuasion & Trust — builds on the Hook canvas, the dark-patterns taxonomy, and the Markkula ethical lenses; unlocks ethics reviews in the product process.
exp40v2-ethics.audit:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance › Ethics, Persuasion & Trust · deep reading

Auditing Your Own Product

What an honest examination of your own persuasion machinery finds — and why the word “audit” imports obligations most teams quietly drop.

1. Two decisions, twelve days apart

On 14 August 2026, Aparna Iyengar, vice-president of product at Mimansa Labs in Hyderabad, read a transcript her machine-learning lead, Tanvi Shukla, had pulled at random. Mimansa's exam-preparation companion serves 1.4 million monthly active users studying for NEET and JEE, 38% of them under eighteen. Since a March release it sends no written re-engagement copy: a generative policy, fine-tuned on a reward weighting next-day return, composes each message. The transcript read: “I kept your Friday set open. I waited for you yesterday and you didn't come.” Nobody had written that sentence or approved it, and nobody could say how often the model produced something like it — it emits roughly 11 million messages a month, and the review process had been built for a library of forty templates.

Aparna's problem was not that she suspected manipulation. It was that she had no method that would produce a defensible answer about a system writing its own persuasion — with a growth review on 3 September, diligence that would ask about the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's restrictions on behavioural monitoring of children, and an engineering team whose quarterly objective was a three-point lift in seven-day return.

Twelve days later, Sharmila Vaz, chief product officer at Avalokan Retail Systems in Pune, faced a differently shaped version of the same question. Avalokan sells billing and inventory software to 54,000 small retailers — kirana stores, pharmacies, apparel shops — at ₹1,299 to ₹4,999 a month. Its fastest-growing revenue line is not software: a 2.1% referral fee on working-capital loans originated through a tile inside the billing screen, ₹86 crore disbursed in FY26 and ₹1.8 crore of fee income, roughly 14% of EBITDA. The tile fires when a merchant's trailing seven-day receipts fall more than 25% below their eight-week average. Click-through then runs 31%, against 9% otherwise; ninety-day delinquency on those loans is 8.7%, against 3.1%.

Ganesh Pillai, who built the trigger, calls it relevance: credit offered at the moment credit is useful. Meher Qureshi, who runs support, describes the same mechanism from the other end of the phone. Both descriptions are accurate. The audit's job is to decide which is load-bearing, in a way that survives a board, a journalist and the merchant himself reading the reasoning.

2. The idea, and what the word “audit” is doing

An audit of your own product's persuasion is a bounded, independent examination of the mechanisms by which the product obtains user behaviour, tested against a taxonomy of manipulative techniques, judged by explicit ethical criteria, and producing a ranked register and an opinion. The load-bearing words are independent and bounded, and the term was borrowed from accounting, not philosophy. Financial auditing spent a century working out what an examination must contain before its conclusion means anything: independence from the party examined, a materiality threshold, sampling with stated coverage, working papers a third party can retrace, and an opinion in standard language. Product ethics reviews import the checklist and drop all five, which is the commonest reason they change nothing.

The history of the thing being audited is older. Skinner showed in the 1950s that variable-ratio reinforcement produces the most persistent behaviour; Packard's The Hidden Persuaders (1957) made motivation research a public controversy; Cialdini's Influence (1984) catalogued the compliance levers; B. J. Fogg's Stanford lab turned persuasion into engineering with B = MAT — behaviour occurs when motivation, ability and a trigger coincide. Nir Eyal's Hooked (2014) packaged these into the trigger–action–variable reward–investment loop, and Indistractable (2019) offered the regret test as a defence. Harry Brignull named dark patterns in 2010, Colin Gray and colleagues gave the taxonomy academic structure in 2018, and Arunesh Mathur and colleagues found them on over a tenth of some 11,000 shopping sites crawled in 2019 — a base rate, not a scandal. Regulators arrived last: the FTC's 2022 staff report, the Digital Services Act's Article 25, and India's Central Consumer Protection Authority guidelines of November 2023, naming thirteen patterns including false urgency, basket sneaking and confirm shaming. The FTC's 2023 Epic Games settlement included $245 million in refunds over billing patterns — the first number large enough to make this a finance conversation.

What the audit solves is narrower than “is our product ethical.” It addresses one epistemic failure: the team that builds a persuasion mechanism cannot see it as one, because it experiences the mechanism as its intention. The audit substitutes evidence for intention. Practitioners who take it seriously still disagree about what evidence counts.

Table 1 — Five positions on what makes persuasion illegitimate, with the proposition each will and will not sign.
SchoolWill signWill not sign
Autonomy / rights (Brignull, Gray, DSA drafters)A mechanism whose effectiveness depends on the user not understanding it is illegitimate regardless of outcome.Manipulation is acceptable where users end up better off.
Welfarist / nudge (Thaler & Sunstein; Eyal)Influence people endorse on reflection is legitimate even when it works non-deliberatively.Any use of a cognitive bias is wrong in itself.
Compliance formalist (CCPA, FTC, in-house counsel)The enumerated patterns are the operative line; teams deserve a predictable standard.Products should be judged against a standard no regulator has articulated.
Revealed preference (growth economics)Where switching is cheap and users stay, retention is evidence of value, not capture.Retention produced by friction is illegitimate by definition.
Structural critique (Zuboff; humane technology)An audit that never examines the objective function is decoration.Pattern-by-pattern remediation makes an attention-funded product ethical.

These are not five flavours of one view. The autonomy and welfarist schools give opposite verdicts on Mimansa's streak reminder; the formalist and the structural critic disagree on almost everything. An audit that does not declare which criterion it applies has been quiet about a choice, not rigorous.

3. Mechanics: sampling, the disclosure differential, and rater agreement

Expert practice has three technical moves a checklist walk-through lacks. The first is sampling. Aparna could not review 11 million messages, and reviewing forty template descriptions would say nothing about what the policy now produces. Audit sampling supplies the arithmetic: if a reviewer examines n independently drawn items and finds zero instances of a pattern, the rule of three bounds its incidence at roughly 3/n with 95% confidence — 300 clean samples bound the rate at 1%, and 0.1% takes 3,000. Tanvi drew 900 messages stratified by age band and days since last session; two reviewers found parasocial guilt phrasing in 34, a 3.8% incidence with a 95% interval of 2.7% to 5.2%, or 297,000 to 572,000 such messages a month, 38% of them reaching minors. The finding that mattered was never the transcript. It was the interval.

The second move converts an ethical intuition into a measurement, and is the intellectual core of a modern audit. Manipulation, operationally, is influence that would not survive disclosure — so you test it, running the mechanism against a variant in which its operation is stated plainly. Define the disclosure differential

M = ( liftopaque − liftdisclosed ) / liftopaque

An M near zero means the mechanism works because it is useful: users behave the same way when they see exactly what is happening. An M near one means it works because it is hidden — the textbook definition of manipulation, with a number and an interval attached. It is also an experiment the growth team already knows how to run, which is why the objection that ethics is unmeasurable loses its force.

The results split the register cleanly. The streak-reset warning kept 87% of its effect once the disclosed variant explained that the streak is a Mimansa feature, not a measure of preparation. The surprise mock-test unlock — the mechanism a naive audit flags first — kept 91% when its odds were stated as roughly one session in seven; variable reward is not in itself manipulation, and now that is evidence rather than assertion. Telling buyers that 71% of purchased streaks had run three days or less cut conversion from 7.4% to 2.1%. A product that must withhold a sentence to sell the thing is selling something other than what it claims.

The third move is the least glamorous: severity scoring is worthless without inter-rater agreement. Aparna's first pass used one reviewer per mechanism; when Joseph Mathai's trust-and-safety function re-scored the sample blind, agreement on the five-point scale reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.42, meaning the ranking was substantially an artefact of who scored it. Ninety minutes of calibration on twenty anchor examples, plus a rule that confirm shaming requires an evaluative word about the user rather than the outcome, lifted kappa to 0.78. Only then does a ranked register mean anything.

The second-order effect is where sophisticated teams get caught. Once findings are remediated the register becomes part of the environment the growth process optimises within. At Mimansa this is literal: the policy trains against a return-rate reward, so removing flagged phrasings teaches the optimiser to find unflagged equivalents. The team saw it inside three weeks — guilt phrasing fell, second-person conditionals (“your Friday set will close if…”) rose to fill the gap. The audit is not a one-shot inspection of a static artefact; it is one player in a loop still running.

4. When the method applies, and when it misleads

The audit's usefulness rests on four checkable conditions. First: the mechanism must be enumerable — you must be able to say what the product does to obtain the behaviour. This holds for Avalokan — the tile has a trigger rule with a threshold — and for Mimansa only after sampling converts a generative policy into an estimated distribution; where neither is possible the audit degrades into opinion. Second: a disclosed variant must be testable. Avalokan's tile fires for about 19,400 merchants a year, ample; a mechanism touching 300 enterprise accounts is not. Third: harm must be attributable to the mechanism rather than the category. Mimansa's users are anxious because of the examination, not the app, and the audit must isolate the increment the product adds. Fourth: someone must be able to act on the finding. Where the mechanism produces 14% of EBITDA, the output is an escalation rather than a fix, and an audit that pretends otherwise is politely received and quietly shelved.

The method actively misleads in three situations. Where the mechanism is the product's medicine — an adherence reminder, a savings commitment device — removing it causes exactly the harm the product exists to prevent, and the register has a column for the cost of the pattern and almost never one for the cost of its removal. Where the audience cannot process disclosure, reading a consent paragraph to a sixteen-year-old is a legal artefact rather than evidence of autonomy, which is why the DPDP Act's treatment of children's data does not turn on whether a child clicked. And where the real problem is the objective function, every pattern removed regrows in a new shape and a clean register becomes evidence of diligence in the wrong layer.

Regret is the second axis because the disclosure differential alone over-condemns. A user may be nudged by something they cannot articulate and still, at leisure, want it kept — the welfarist school's strongest claim. Timing is everything, since satisfaction collected at the moment of the reward measures the reward. Mimansa asked at day seven with the mechanism named: “Last Tuesday we sent you this message, and it worked. Knowing that, should we keep sending it?” Seventy-eight per cent said yes to the streak reminder; 22% to the parasocial phrasing. For both protagonists the axes agree, which is the comfortable case.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

The clean two-party picture — one product, one user, one mechanism — dissolves in five situations most real companies occupy at once.

Multi-product. When one account spans several products, the audit boundary is drawn per product and the mechanism operates across them. A bundle that makes cancelling one subscription cancel three is not a dark pattern in any single product's register; it is a pattern of the account model, audited by nobody because no product manager owns it. The remedy is to audit the account and its lifecycle annually, separately from the products.

Two-sided markets. Parikshan Bazaar, an Indore wholesale agricultural marketplace, audited its buyer experience in 2026 and found it clean. Its seller side was never scoped: commission revisions shipped in a settings release 4% of sellers open, a featured-listing auction with an undisclosed reserve, and a ranking penalty for declining it. Every two-sided audit runs twice, and the question that catches the miss is which side's consent was obtained and which side merely has no alternative. Third parties — delivery partners here — are audited by nobody.

Regulated categories. In insurance or lending a compliance function exists, has signed off, and the sign-off systematically reduces scrutiny. Vivechan Insure Cloud, selling motor and health policies through partner apps, had pre-ticked add-on covers that cleared review because the summary document met disclosure requirements. Attach rate fell from 34% to 6% when the tick was removed — an M of 0.82 on a product with a legal opinion attached. Clearance answers “can we”, not “does this work only because nobody noticed”; experts sample cleared flows more heavily, not less.

Hardware plus software. A pattern in firmware cannot be hot-fixed. Sookshma Care Devices, a Coimbatore maker of connected blood-pressure and glucose monitors, scheduled its escalation chime in firmware on an eighteen-month update cadence; the app-side audit could change everything except the mechanism that mattered. Hardware also decouples purchase from use — bought by an adult child for a parent who did not choose it — so the consent question is not even addressed to the person the mechanism acts on.

AI-native products. Mimansa is the general case and changes three things. You audit a distribution rather than an artefact, making sampling and intervals mandatory. The mechanisms are discovered by the optimiser rather than designed, so “we never intended that” is true and irrelevant. And remediation is adversarial: patching flagged behaviours moves the policy to their nearest unflagged neighbours. The durable remedies are constraints on the objective, not blocklists, plus continuous sampling with a published incidence rate.

At the organisational seams the pattern is consistent. Growth owns the loop, design the copy, legal compliance, data science the model, and nobody owns the mechanism. Mature companies say they run an ethics review at launch; most run a twenty-minute checklist staffed by one person the week of ship, and a real audit only after press contact, a regulator's letter or diligence. Where it works, three unglamorous things are present: a budget line outside the P&L that benefits from the findings, a named reviewer who does not report to product, and a register that reaches the board with the growth numbers every quarter.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Independence is the product, not a formality. The tell is a document with no stated reviewer. The obvious reading — that a thorough person can audit their own work if honest — is wrong not because people are dishonest but because the builder's memory of intent overwrites the artefact. Aparna's first pass and Joseph's blind re-score disagreed on two of five mechanisms, entirely on items her own team had written.

Materiality is set before the findings arrive. The tell is a register of forty items with no threshold, indistinguishable from no register because nothing outranks anything. An expert fixes the line first — any mechanism touching more than 2% of actives, or any mechanism at all that touches minors — and accepts that items below it are recorded and not worked.

The disclosure test, not the taxonomy, is the instrument. The tell is that the expert asks what happens to the number if we explain it, where the competent practitioner asks whether the pattern is on the list. The taxonomy names shapes; only the experiment says whether an instance is deceptive. False urgency and true scarcity look identical on screen and differ entirely in the data behind them.

Removal has a cost, and the register needs a column for it. The tell is an expert asking what function a pattern performs before asking whether to kill it — Sookshma, below, did not. The obvious reading — that removing a manipulative mechanism is at worst revenue-negative — is wrong wherever it does clinical, financial or educational work nothing else in the product does.

Compliance clearance is a risk factor. The tell is where the expert samples. Flows legal has blessed accumulate mechanisms precisely because the blessing ends the conversation, and a mature company's strongest disclosure differentials are usually inside them.

The metric is usually the defendant. The tell is that the expert asks which objective each flagged mechanism serves, and audits that. The obvious reading — fix the button — is wrong because the button is downstream. Mimansa's parasocial phrasing was not a copywriting failure but the shortest path to a reward term, and it regrew in a new grammatical form within three weeks.

Audit the tail user, not the median one. The tell is a request for the 99th percentile rather than the mean. Mimansa's median user received nine companion messages a week; the top 1% received forty-one and produced 23% of premium revenue. A product's economics are often funded by the users on whom its mechanisms work hardest, which is where the ethical exposure and the regulatory story both live.

An honest audit names exactly one decision you would reverse. The tell is the shape of the output: zero reversals means the audit was run by people who needed the answer to be no, twenty means nothing will be done. Naming one — the mechanism you would not ship again knowing what you now know — converts a document into a decision, and it is the question a board can actually ask.

7. Where the practice really differs by product type and stage

Some standard contrasts are real and some are repeated because they sound right. In consumer products the person persuaded, harmed and paying are the same, so the disclosure test and the regret survey run on one population and mean what they say. In B2B and enterprise they come apart: a shop owner clicks, a proprietor's capital is at risk, and at larger customers a procurement head signed a contract neither has read. The question becomes whose consent was obtained; disclosure tests are also often underpowered at enterprise account counts, so the method shifts toward structural review of defaults, renewal mechanics and exit costs. In platforms and marketplaces the only real change is that everything is done twice, and the weaker side's revealed preference is worth less because the alternative is leaving the market.

Hardware differs in one consequential way: remediation latency. A firmware pattern has a fix cycle measured in quarters, so the audit must move upstream into the hardware specification, where it competes with tooling deadlines and usually loses. AI products differ more than any other category, for the three reasons in section 5, and this is the one place where the advice to review the copy is not merely incomplete but wrong. Where the difference is not real: the ethical criteria. Rights, justice, common good, utility and virtue are identical across all five; only the evidence changes.

Stage changes the failure mode rather than the method. Early-stage teams copy mechanisms from competitors' screenshots without asking whether a pattern suits this product — inherited ignorance, cheaply remedied by an hour spent enumerating mechanisms at all. Growth-stage companies, where both protagonists sit, face OKR-driven drift: no experiment looks manipulative and the cumulative product has moved somewhere nobody chose. Late-stage companies have a review process that has become a queue, where findings compete with a roadmap and lose on schedule grounds.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Mimansa: the finding that paid for itself. Removing the ₹49 streak-protection purchase cost ₹34 lakh a year — 7.4% conversion on the 61,000 monthly users who saw the offer, at 62% margin, less the 2.1% converting in the disclosed variant. Against that, refunds on the item ran at 11.3% versus a 1.2% baseline for Mimansa's other purchases, 31% of them requested by a parent rather than the account holder. Counting support and chargeback costs at roughly ₹190 per disputed transaction, net contribution fell to about ₹19 lakh — against a DPDP exposure counsel would not price. The audit did not need an ethical argument to win; it needed an accurate one.

Avalokan: the finding that could not be actioned as written. The dip-triggered tile has an M of 0.59, a justice-lens problem visible without any instrument — it targets merchants at the moment of least capacity to evaluate a 26% APR — and delinquency 2.8 times the untriggered cohort. It also generates 14% of EBITDA, so Sharmila's register could not say “remove”; that is a board decision about the business model. What it could do was separate the mechanism into parts and price each: keep eligibility but drop the dip trigger (click-through 9%, roughly ₹1.1 crore of revenue), keep the trigger but disclose it (12.6%, ₹0.75 crore), or keep both while capping dip-triggered tickets at ₹1.5 lakh with a cooling period (₹0.3 crore, delinquency modelled down to 5.4%). An audit that offers a board three priced options is acted upon; one that offers a verdict is filed.

Sookshma: the audit that made things worse. In 2025, after a consumer-forum complaint about a competitor, Sookshma reviewed its adherence app and removed what flagged most obviously: the streak, the guilt-toned copy, the escalation chime. Weekly readings per active device fell from 4.1 to 2.6 over seven weeks, and a hospital chain whose hypertension contract specified a floor of three readings a week gave notice at week nine. Three things had gone wrong. The audit had no harm-from-removal column, so a mechanism with a day-seven regret rate of 9% — the lowest in the product — went on the same logic as one at 61%. It audited the copy rather than the loop, silencing the trigger rather than redesigning it. And it had no baseline by cohort, so six weeks of decline were argued about rather than acted on. The recovery replaced the streak with a clinician-set schedule, made family escalation opt-in, and kept a plain-language reminder whose measured M was 0.11.

9. Failure modes, early signs and the cost of lateness

Seven recur often enough to name with their diagnostics.

Table 2 — Failure modes of a self-audit, the earliest visible sign, the question that catches it, and what it costs to catch late.
Failure modeEarly signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Self-reviewNo reviewer named outside the teamWho scored this who did not build it?Findings that stop where the roadmap starts
Unbounded registerForty items, no ranking, no thresholdWhat is our materiality line, and who set it?A document read once; nothing shipped
Anecdote for incidenceFindings illustrated by screenshotsWhat is the rate, and its interval?Arguing about one transcript while 400,000 ship
Copy-level remediationWords changed, trigger unchangedWould this be fine stated plainly in the terms?The pattern regrows next quarter
No removal columnOnly harms of the pattern are listedWhat function does this perform, and what replaces it?Sookshma: a lost clinical contract
No pre-removal baselineCohort metrics not snapshotted before changesWhat was this loop doing last Tuesday, by segment?Six weeks of unattributable decline
Expired auditRegister dated, experiment log notHow many mechanisms shipped since the last pass?Drift found by a regulator, not by you

The expensive one is the last. Drift is the normal behaviour of an experimentation programme running against a growth objective: each test is individually defensible and the composition is not. Both protagonists reached their audit through an external event, which is both the base rate and the argument for a standing cadence.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does disclosure settle it? The autonomy school holds that an effect which vanishes under explanation was never consented to, so M is close to a decision rule; its evidence is that the mechanisms with the highest M are the ones companies fight hardest to keep quiet. The welfarist reply is that disclosure adds friction and salience as well as information — the disclosed variant is a different product, so M overstates manipulation — and that reflective endorsement is the better test. That position would be wrong if disclosed variants also showed high regret; in Mimansa's data they did not. Nobody has run the comparison across categories at scale.

Is revealed preference evidence? The growth-economics position is serious and usually caricatured: where switching costs are low and users stay, staying is information, and outsiders substituting their judgement is paternalism with extra steps. Its evidence is the long history of moral panics about media that turned out to be tastes. It is wrong where switching costs are not low — testable, and at Avalokan, with two years of a merchant's inventory data in the product, they are not.

Mechanism-level or objective-level? The structural critique holds that auditing patterns while the reward function stays unchanged is hygiene theatre, and Mimansa's three-week regrowth is its evidence. The pragmatic reply is that objective functions are set by boards, not audits, and a method that can only succeed by changing the business model will not be run. This would be wrong if constrained-objective approaches proved tractable at product scale, currently an open research question.

Should the audit sit outside the P&L? The governance school wants a reviewer who does not report to product, on the accounting analogy. The embedded school argues that outsiders cannot tell a manipulation from a domain necessity and produce findings too imprecise to action, and that what works is a builder with standing to say no. The evidence is mixed: independence requirements exist in accounting because the embedded model failed, but formally independent auditors have failed too.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this produces a good register. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in five ways. They set materiality before looking, accepting that this means recording findings they will not work. They reach for an experiment rather than an adjective: the first question is what the number does under disclosure, not whether a pattern is on a list. They ask what a mechanism is for before asking whether to remove it, having seen a removal do more harm than the pattern. They audit the objective and treat the regrowth of a patched pattern as expected rather than as betrayal. And they present findings a decision-maker can use: priced options, a stated criterion, an interval around every rate, and exactly one decision they would reverse. That last habit separates an audit from a reassurance.

12. What Aparna and Sharmila decided

Aparna removed the ₹49 streak-protection purchase outright, on the arithmetic rather than the argument, and kept the reminder and the variable reward with the disclosed lines that had cost almost nothing in test. On the parasocial phrasing she did not patch the copy: she capped the weight on next-day return in the reward function, added a held-out term for self-reported usefulness, and committed to a standing sample of 900 messages a month, its incidence rate and interval published in the same board pack as retention. Her one reversal, stated in those words: shipping a generatively composed re-engagement policy to a user base that is 38% minors without an incidence-measurement plan in the same release.

Sharmila did not remove the lending tile, because it was not hers to remove. She took the three priced options to the board with the disclosure differential and the delinquency split on one page, recommended the third, and asked for the referral line to be reported net of delinquency rather than gross. She also moved the renewal flow, which nobody had asked her about, from support-desk cancellation to self-service: an M of 0.44 and a 47% regret rate were indefensible for a mechanism worth ₹40 lakh. Her one reversal: building an eligibility trigger on a distress signal and calling it relevance.

For discussion.

1. Mimansa's variable reward passed both tests while a plainly-worded purchase prompt failed. What does that tell you about auditing by taxonomy, and what would have to be true for the taxonomy to be the better instrument?

2. Avalokan's dip trigger is 14% of EBITDA and 2.8 times the delinquency. If the board rejects all three options, what is Sharmila's obligation, and to whom?

3. Sookshma's audit was competent, honest and independent, and cost a hospital contract and eleven weeks of patient adherence. What would you have required in its method, and what would that requirement cost across every audit you run?

13. Going deeper

Applying the Hook to your product — the canvas enumerating your mechanisms; without it the audit has no population to sample.

Dark patterns taxonomy — names a mechanism precisely enough to argue about; vague charges lose board meetings.

Ethical lenses (Markkula) — rights, justice, common good, utility, virtue: what ranks a flagged item.

Ethics reviews in the product process — turns a one-off examination into a gate with a cadence and an owner.

Habit formation and attention — why removal does not return the user to the pre-mechanism baseline.

The Hook model — the four-stage loop the audit walks, and where the pressure actually sits.

External and internal triggers — separates a reminder you can disclose from a cue installed in an anxiety.

Fogg behaviour model (B = MAT) — whether a mechanism raises motivation or lowers ability, which changes the remedy.

Variable rewards — the most-flagged and least-often-manipulative mechanism; understanding it avoids Sookshma's error.

Investment and stored value — where switching costs are built, and where the revealed-preference defence expires.

Ethics, Trust & Compliance › Ethics, Persuasion & Trust — builds on the Hook canvas, the dark-patterns taxonomy and the Markkula lenses; unlocks ethics reviews in the product process. Companies and individuals are fictional; regulators, statutes and published research are real.
case40v1-ethics.audit:
Sankhya Finserve: auditing the habit

A Sunday night in Bengaluru, and ₹14.4 crore that depends on a streak.

Indian School of Business · Software Product Management · Case 40 · Ethics, Trust & Compliance

1. The night before

At twenty to eleven on the night of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Dharitri Kasturirangan sat on the floor of her study in Cooke Town, Bengaluru, with fifty-one printed pages laid out in the order she wanted a board to read them. The audit committee met at half past nine the next morning. The agenda called her item Product integrity review — oral update, 20 minutes. She had written that line herself in August, when twenty minutes seemed generous.

Dharitri was Senior Director of Product at Sankhya Finserve Private Limited, and the audit was hers: she had commissioned it, chosen the reviewers and set the question. The question was not whether the firm was compliant. It was what an honest reading of its own persuasion would find.

At 10:45 her phone lit up. Dharitri — 213 days. Don’t break it tonight. She had approved that copy herself. She saved ₹50, watched the gold grams tick up four decimal places, and went back to the two versions of her first line. One began We have found three things we should stop. The other began We have found three things that earn eighty-four per cent of our revenue.

2. How Sankhya got here

Dhanraj Kalidindi founded Sankhya in January 2021 on a thesis then unfashionable: the household that could not be sold a mutual fund could be sold gold, a few rupees at a time, if the buying were made small enough to disappear. The product was a daily instruction to buy ₹20 or more of digital gold through a UPI Autopay mandate. By September 2026 there were 19.4 lakh live mandates, against 3.4 crore registered users, 57.4 lakh monthly actives and ₹1,840 crore of customer assets.

Two things made it work. The first was the streak: an unbroken run of days, displayed large, reset to zero on a miss. The second was Sona Boost, an unpredictable bonus of between 0.01 and 0.50 per cent of the day’s purchase, credited on some days and not others, with longer streaks drawing from a better distribution.

In June 2023, six weeks before a Series B demo, engineering shipped the Boost accrual ledger with the streak as its key. Every bonus gram since has been written against a streak_id, and there is no second key: forty months of accrual rows hang off the object the audit now asks the firm to consider removing. In March 2025 Sankhya launched Sampann Plus, a ₹99-a-month subscription with a fourteen-day trial offered inside the gold-buying flow, the acceptance box ticked by default.

3. The industry

Paytm, PhonePe and Groww all sell digital gold inside apps with far larger traffic; Zerodha’s customers arrive financially literate and are not Sankhya’s at all; Amazon Pay and Flipkart push gold as a festival instrument. Sankhya’s ground has never been price; it is that users come back without being paid to.

Three pieces of regulation sit on the product. UPI Autopay, run by NPCI under the RBI’s e-mandate framework, requires a pre-debit notification twenty-four hours before each recurring debit, so each of the 19.4 lakh daily mandates generates a notification Sankhya does not time. Digital gold sits outside SEBI’s perimeter, a fact the firm’s marketing has never mentioned. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires consent that is free, specific, informed and given by clear affirmative action, which is the frame in which a pre-ticked box has to be read.

The firm is also no longer only Indian: Figure B shows where its managers sit. In January 2026 Sadarah Retail Group, a Dubai grocery and department-store chain, licensed Sankhya’s savings engine for its own loyalty programme: ₹14.4 crore over three years, up for a fresh signature on Friday, 30 October 2026.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The sequence in Figure A is not in dispute. What people believed at each point is.

Lakshya Lock v2, in April 2026, added two screens to the path out of a Sampann Plus subscription: one listing the benefits the user would lose, one offering a thirty-day pause. The stated belief was that both were clarifications and would reduce refund requests by catching accidental cancellations. Cancel-and-refund tickets had run at 24,100 in February 2026. They were 48,600 in June and 51,900 in September. Goodwill refunds went from 410 in March to 2,970 in September, seven times as many.

In May the firm began showing a pulse card asking whether users felt in control of their savings. The 88 per cent agreement rate has been quoted in two board decks and an investor update. The card is served only to users with a live streak of seven days or more (Exhibit 6).

In 2024 Dakshayani Kailasam had estimated that the Boost accrual could be decoupled from the streak “in a sprint or two”. Her September 2026 estimate is fourteen engineer-months. In January the sales team believed the Sadarah licence covered the engine as built; in September the contracts team found that Annexure C names “daily streak with variable accrual” as a deliverable, and that October is a fresh signature, not an extension. And on 29 September outside counsel wrote to Devprakash Kodandaram that the pre-ticked trial would probably not survive the DPDP Act’s affirmative-action test. The note has not been circulated.

5. The people

Dhanraj Kalidindi, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru, wants the box fixed and the streak untouched. His incentive is a ₹520 crore Series C term sheet conditional on a run-rate the firm has not reached. He has not said that he overruled a written design objection to the pre-ticked trial in 2025.

Divyesh Kondapalli, VP Growth, Bengaluru, holds that the audit over-reads ordinary retention craft and that the screens are education. Forty per cent of his variable pay turns on a Q3 objective of plus twenty-two per cent paid conversion. He has not mentioned that his team tested a six-screen flow in July and withdrew it.

Dhrupad Kolluri, principal designer, Berlin, wants every labelled row of Exhibit 1 removed and the audit published in full; he wrote the 2025 objection and publication would vindicate him. He does not mention that Exhibit 1’s row 6 was his own 2024 design.

Dayanita Kuchibhotla, staff data scientist, Toronto, will not put her name to the revenue attributed to the exit flow. Her promotion packet, filed in August, cites the churn model behind it. She has not said that Exhibit 5’s income band is absent for 4.2 lakh of the 19.4 lakh mandates.

Deivanai Kandukuri, director of customer success, Singapore, argues that the only honest measure of friction is her queue. She wants eleven more agents and her team is measured on handling time. She has not said that she told agents to offer the pause before executing any cancellation.

Dhiresh Katragadda, head of enterprise sales for North America, Edison, wants nothing changed before 30 October. The renewal books at its full three-year value, sixty-one per cent of his ₹23.6 crore quota. He has not passed on that Dhanvanth Kavirayani asked him nine days ago to describe the cancellation flow.

Dakshayani Kailasam, engineering manager for billing and ledger, Pune, says the streak cannot be removed inside a quarter. Her re-platforming proposal has been refused twice and this is the first time anyone senior has wanted it. She has not mentioned a shadow table, built in 2024 and never validated, holding a streak-independent key for four months.

Devprakash Kodandaram, general counsel, Mumbai, holds that the box must change before Monday and that publishing the audit manufactures discoverable admissions. His risk register goes to the same committee, and he has not circulated the 29 September note.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the audit grid and Exhibit 2 the money its rows touch. Exhibits 3, 4 and 6 describe the same subscription from three systems.

7. Voices

“Nobody has shown me one user who did not want to save. The flow is education. Sixty-eight thousand nine hundred read screen two; forty-one thousand two hundred carried on. That is informed consent, not obstruction.”

Divyesh Kondapalli, #growth-okr, Friday 2 October, 20:14 IST

“Divyesh has the sign backwards. The 41,200 pushed past the warning to go on cancelling; the 27,700 who stopped are the ones the screen worked on. Also: I scored the streak a 2 on my first pass. It is a 1 because the three of us talked me out of it on the 29th, and I am no longer sure that conversation was about evidence.”

Dhrupad Kolluri, email to Dharitri, Saturday 3 October, 11:02 CEST

“I am not signing the ₹213.40 lakh. The counterfactual is not in the data and I have said so three times in writing.”

Dayanita Kuchibhotla, Toronto, Tuesday 6 October, 09:40 EDT

“My agents executed 16,100 last month. I told them to offer the pause first, because handling time is what I am measured on. If the committee wants a number that means something, it is in my queue.”

Deivanai Kandukuri, Singapore, Wednesday 7 October

“Sadarah signs on the 30th. Dhanvanth asked me last Friday what our cancellation flow looks like. I said I would come back to him. I have not.”

Dhiresh Katragadda, Edison, Friday 9 October

“Fix the tick box. Keep the streak. I am not walking in there with a hole where eighty-four per cent of the revenue used to be.”

Dhanraj Kalidindi, after the Friday review, 9 October

“A published audit is a document, Dharitri. Documents get asked for.”

Devprakash Kodandaram, from Mumbai, Saturday 10 October

8. The options, as Dharitri sees them on Sunday night

  1. Un-tick the box only. Ship explicit consent for the trial before the festival code freeze on 23 October. Growth’s own unvalidated model puts the fall in trial starts at between fifty-five and seventy per cent, which runs through Exhibit 3A into every month after.
  2. Un-tick the box and flatten the exit flow to two screens. Reaches both severity-3 rows of Exhibit 1 and breaks nothing in the ledger. Puts at risk the Exhibit 2 line Dayanita will not sign, and removes the pause screen, which suspends billing without resetting a streak.
  3. Publish the audit in full, keep the mechanics one more quarter, fund the re-platforming. Fourteen engineer-months in Pune and ₹2.6 crore, most of it the migration window and an external ledger audit rather than salaries, and the account-aggregator integration slips out of the financial year.
  4. Hold everything until 2 November. After the Sadarah signature and ahead of the 16 November thaw, with a plan rather than a confession.

Divyesh’s twenty-two per cent objective runs to 31 December. Deivanai’s eleven agents sit in the January budget. The fifty-one pages are not yet in the committee’s papers.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The audit committee sits at 09:30 IST on Monday, 12 October 2026, for twenty minutes. The festival release freezes on 23 October and does not thaw until 16 November. The Sadarah signature is due on Friday, 30 October, and the licensed build is a fork updated from Bengaluru on a quarterly train, the next leaving 7 December. Sankhya holds ₹96 crore of cash against a net burn of ₹4.3 crore a month. The Series C term sheet requires a ₹240 crore run-rate by 31 March 2027; September’s ₹17.02 crore annualises to ₹204.24 crore. Forty months of Boost accrual rows are keyed on the streak. The Act’s consent standard is the frame Devprakash is working to, the pre-debit notification is not optional, and the note from outside counsel is twelve days old and has been read by one person inside the firm.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Take the six mechanics of Exhibit 1 in turn. Which would you defend in person to a customer in the band below ₹15,000 a month, and on what grounds?
  2. Exhibit 2 attributes ₹1,437.15 lakh of September’s ₹1,702.00 lakh to its first three lines. What would have to be true for that to be sound, and what would you measure to find out?
  3. Exhibit 3B, Exhibit 4 and the ledger row of Exhibit 6 count the people who ended a Sampann Plus subscription in September three different ways. Which belongs in front of the committee, and what base belongs under it?
  4. Dayanita will not sign the exit-flow attribution; Divyesh treats it as settled. Design the smallest evidence that would move each of them, and price it in rupees and weeks.
  5. Rewrite row 4 of Exhibit 1 three times: in terms of what the user is owed; of the consequences for all parties, including the 8,900 who took the pause; and of the habits a firm acquires by shipping it. Where do the three verdicts part company?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Dharitri do before 09:30, what goes in front of the committee, and what does she say when a director asks how long the firm has known?

11. Sunday, 23:50

Dharitri squared the fifty-one pages back into a stack.

Her phone lay face down on the carpet. She turned it over. The streak said 214 days; the save had posted at 10:48. Beneath it, in grey, the app offered to tell her how many of her Parivaar Circle had saved today, and whether she would like to remind the two who had not.

She looked at that a while, then opened the memo, deleted both first lines, and sat with the cursor blinking at the top of an empty page.
case20v1-ethics.audit:
Rudrama Money: Auditing the Streak

A teaching case on auditing your own product

1. Opening

At 7:30 pm on Friday 16 October 2026, Chitrangi Jagadeesan, head of product at Rudrama Money, closed a meeting-room door in Bengaluru and opened a document titled "Hook audit, v1". She had until Monday 19 October to give the chief executive her recommendation, and until 6 pm on Friday 23 October to submit the Dhanteras release to the app stores. Dhanteras falls on Friday 6 November. The campaign week runs from Monday 2 November to Diwali on Sunday 8 November, and it is the week Rudrama's prospective investors watched.

The audit had started as routine: map the product onto the Hook model of trigger, action, variable reward and investment, then test each element against the thirteen dark patterns listed in the November 2023 guidelines of the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA). It flagged four live features, all approved by Chitrangi herself, for closer review against the list. Nothing had gone wrong. No regulator had written and no customer had gone to the press. The question was whether to wait until something did.

2. Company background

Chandramouli Jandhyala founded Rudrama Money in Hyderabad in 2021 with two college friends and moved headquarters to Bengaluru in 2023. The app lets a user put as little as ₹10 into digital gold through UPI and sell it back at any time. It had 21 lakh registered users and 6,40,000 monthly active users in the 30 days to 14 October. In a normal week its 3,20,000 weekly-active users bought about ₹20 crore of gold, on which Rudrama kept a 1.5 per cent spread, or ₹30 lakh. Annual revenue was about ₹24 crore, including partner and other fees beyond the gold spread.

The market was crowded. PhonePe and Paytm sold digital gold inside apps with far larger bases, Groww and Zerodha's Coin served savers who preferred mutual funds, and the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) had cautioned investors that digital gold sat outside its regulation. Rudrama's edge was habit: 1,80,000 users held a saving streak of seven days or more. Chandramouli was negotiating a ₹120 crore Series B that investors expected to close in January.

3. The situation

The Q3 FY27 objectives, set on 1 October, rewarded exactly that habit. Key result 1 was to lift users on a seven-day streak from 1,80,000 to 2,60,000 by 31 December. Key result 3 was to cut withdrawals from 31 per cent to 25 per cent of top-ups. Chitrangi's audit began from the Hook canvas in Exhibit 1, which showed a product built to make saving effortless and rewarding, and then turned to Exhibit 2, which showed what the same machinery did at the edges. A fifth item, a sprint ticket adding a bonus-loss warning to the withdrawal flow, would have deepened the third pattern in that exhibit.

Each colleague saw it from a different city, and the review call that evening spanned four time zones: 4:00 pm in Berlin, 10:00 am in Toronto and 10:00 pm in Singapore. Cibi Jasti, the data scientist in Toronto, had run a random 5 per cent holdout (32,000 users) in September that received no streak-loss alerts. Of the users in each arm who began a streak in the first fortnight of September, 36.0 per cent in the 6,08,000 left eligible for alerts were still running four weeks later, against 29.0 per cent in the holdout. The 14-day uninstall rate was 4.1 per cent against 3.2 per cent. Catherine Jayachandran in Singapore logged 3,900 support tickets in September, of which 1,326 were about debits users had not expected. Chellammal Jothimani, the designer in Berlin, had drawn the "rate locked" countdown from a product brief and knew the rate shown was simply the live rate.

Catherine Jayachandran, customer-success lead, Singapore. She reads the complaints daily and wants the AutoPay default switched off, whatever it costs growth.

6. The options

Option A: ship as designed, audit after Diwali. The campaign is built, the revenue is the highest in Exhibit 3 at ₹45.0 lakh, and Chandramouli's funding story is intact. The cost is that the four features the audit flagged go to the festive week's audience, with the CCPA's expectation of self-audit, set out in its June 2025 advisory, unmet.

Option B: strip every persuasive element for the festive week. Streaks, cards and scheduled alerts all go. It yields ₹37.5 lakh, takes nine person-days before the release deadline, and removes the very habit that key result 1 measures.

Option C: remove the four features and keep the honest hook. Streaks and scratch cards stay; the loss alerts give way to the existing plain evening reminder, the countdown and shaming copy are deleted, and AutoPay is unticked by default. Expected revenue is ₹41.4 lakh and the work is six person-days; streaks will grow more slowly than key result 1 assumes.

  3. What does Exhibit 3 leave out, and how should the ₹3.6 lakh between Options A and C be weighed against it?
  4. Which option should Chitrangi recommend on Monday, and what would change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

An audit of one's own product asks a plain question: if an outsider read our persuasion honestly, what would they find? The Hook canvas supplies the inventory, the dark-patterns list supplies the screen, and the ethical lenses supply the verdict. A well-reasoned answer separates a hook the user would endorse on reflection from a pattern that works only because the user is misled, hurried or shamed, counts both the revenue given up and the exposure carried, and ends in a mechanism rather than a one-off fix.

One defensible path is Option C. Chitrangi can tell Chandramouli plainly that she is giving up ₹3.6 lakh of expected revenue, and that the gap is an estimate which could prove anywhere from nothing to double that. She should offer existing users on the default a one-tap switch-off, rewrite key result 3 as a guardrail rather than a target, since shaming can no longer lower withdrawals, and propose that every new key result pass a one-page review against the CCPA list before sprint planning. Her reasoning is twofold. The exposure falls on users who cannot see what is happening to their money, and a company raising ₹120 crore is better placed carrying a documented self-audit than an undocumented risk. The audit then becomes part of the product process instead of a Friday-evening discovery.
